hook.line: Tomás's new room is small, the rent is high, and the shower works one day in three. To complain properly he needs more than *muy* and *mucho*: he needs quite and too.
hook.es: El cuarto es bastante bonito, pero el arriendo es demasiado caro.
hook.en: The room is quite nice, but the rent is too expensive.

examples.es: Hay mucha gente en la calle.
examples.en: There are a lot of people in the street.

rule:
You already have *muy*, *mucho* and *poco*. Two more words fill in the scale:

*poco*: not much
*bastante*: quite a lot, or enough
*mucho*: a lot
*demasiado*: too much

They work in three spots, just like *mucho*.

Before a thing, they match it. *Demasiado* takes all four endings: *demasiado café*, *demasiada gente*, *demasiados carros*, *demasiadas cosas*. *Bastante* only adds an *s*: *bastante tiempo*, *bastantes sillas*.

Before a describing word, they never change: *bastante caro*, *demasiado pequeña*. This is the spot where *mucho* turns into *muy*.

After a verb, they never change either: *trabajo bastante*, *habla demasiado*.

Careful with too: *demasiado* is a complaint, more than you want. Very expensive is *muy caro*; too expensive to pay is *demasiado caro*.
smallPrint: Teachers call these quantifiers. In front of a noun they agree with it; in front of an adjective or after a verb they work as adverbs and stay fixed.

options: There are a lot of people today.
There are too many people today.
I have quite a lot of time.
I drink a lot of coffee.
I drink quite a lot of coffee.

readAndPick.es: Hay demasiadas mesas en el café.
options: There are too many tables in the café.
There are a lot of tables in the café.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Hay ___ gente en el café.* (*demasiado* or *demasiada*) There are too many people in the café.
yourTurn.answer: Hay demasiada gente en el café.
accept: En el café hay demasiada gente.
yourTurn.why: Before a thing it matches, and *gente* is feminine: *demasiada*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *El arriendo es ___ caro.* (*muy* or *mucho*) The rent is very expensive.
yourTurn.why: Before a describing word, *mucho* turns into *muy*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *El cuarto es ___ pequeño.* (*bastante* or *bastantes*) The room is quite small.
yourTurn.why: Before a describing word nothing changes, so no *s*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I work quite a lot.
yourTurn.why: After a verb, *bastante* stays as it is.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I have too many things.
Ask a friend: Do you have enough time?
yourTurn.why: Enough of a thing is *bastante*, and *tiempo* takes the plain form.

yourTurn.prompt: Turn the complaint up: *El café es muy caro.* Say it's too expensive.
yourTurn.why: More than you want is *demasiado*, and before a describing word it doesn't change.
The verb changes for Hernando; *demasiado* after a verb stays the same.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Before a thing, *demasiado* matches it, and *gente* is feminine.
Before a describing word *demasiado* never changes, even next to a feminine one.
Before a plural thing, *bastante* adds an *s*.

pitfalls.wrong: El pan de Vale es demasiado bueno.
pitfalls.right: El pan de Vale es muy bueno.
pitfalls.why: *Demasiado* means more than you want. For a compliment, use *muy*.

personal: Describe your own home honestly in three lines: one thing that's *bastante* good, one thing that's *demasiado* something, and one thing there's *poco* of.
